Empirical Research Plan: “Do Governance Arrangements Destroy Value in Corporate Acquisitions?”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Chosen method: Two–stage least squares (IV) with an event–study outcome.

Why IV is appropriate  
• The outcome we care about—announcement-period cumulative abnormal return (CAR)—is short-horizon, so reverse causality (bad acquisitions causing firms to change their charter last week) is negligible.  
• However, the principal regressor—managerial insulation (G-index, staggered board, etc.)—is clearly endogenous: able managers may voluntarily keep themselves exposed; entrenched managers may load up on defenses; adoption can correlate with unobservable firm culture.  
• We therefore need a source of plausibly exogenous variation in insulation.  Two instruments supply this:

 1. State antitakeover statutes (SATS): whether the acquirer’s state of incorporation has a business-combination, control-share cash-out, poison-pill endorsement, or fair-price statute in force in year t.  Many of these laws were enacted by state legislatures for political rather than firm-specific reasons, and several were amended during 1990-2003, providing within-state-year variation.

 2. Peer inertia: the lagged average G-index of other listed firms incorporated in the same state (or 3-digit SIC) × year, excluding the focal firm.  Charters are costly to amend; thus a high “ambient” level of defenses in the local legal/product market environment predicts a high firm-level G without being affected by the focal firm’s current acquisition plan.

The combination of SATS and peer inertia yields a powerful first stage and allows over-identification tests.

Model sketch  
First-stage: GIndex_i,t  = π_0 + π_1 SATS_s,t  + π_2 PeerG_sic,state,t-1 + X_i,t π + ϑ_i + ϕ_t + u_i,t  
Second-stage: CAR_{–1,+1} = β·Ĝ_i,t + X_i,t γ + ϑ_i + ϕ_t + ε_i,t

with firm FE ϑ_i and calendar-year FE ϕ_t.  Standard errors two-way-clustered by firm and year.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
• Treatment variable: Managerial insulation, proxied chiefly by (i) continuous G-index and (ii) a binary “High Protection” indicator = 1 if G-index ≥ 14 (top tercile in Gompers–Ishii–Metrick 2003) or if the firm has a staggered board.

• Control group: Firms with G-index ≤ 5 (bottom tercile) / firms without a staggered board.

• Event date: Acquisition announcement; outcome window is CAR[–1,+1] trading days.

• Instrument timing: SATS_s,t equals 1 beginning the fiscal year the statute becomes effective; PeerG is lagged one year to prevent mechanical simultaneity.

(No running variable → not RDD.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1 Instrument relevance: SATS and PeerG materially predict the firm’s takeover defenses (first-stage F > 10).  Plausible; prior literature shows 5–10-point G-index jumps after business-combination statutes.

A2 Exclusion restriction: Conditional on controls and fixed effects, SATS and PeerG affect acquisition CAR only through their impact on the firm’s own takeover vulnerability, not through alternative channels (e.g., macro shocks).  Reasonable because:  
 • SATS are broad, not deal-specific.  
 • Peer charters per se do not influence the specific acquirer’s stock price once we hold constant industry-year shocks with FE.

A3 Stable unit treatment (no spillovers): The treatment status of firm j does not affect firm i’s CAR within a three-day window.  Short windows make cross-firm price spillovers unlikely.

A4 No differential time trends after conditioning on year FE and controls: Any secular governance or M&A cycle trends are absorbed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1 Self-selection into state of incorporation.  
 • Fix: Include firm fixed effects (many firms stay in the same state), and test robustness on the subsample of firms incorporated in Delaware (little variation in location but variation in PeerG).

T2 SATS may influence bidder-competition environment (e.g., rival bidders incorporated in same state).  
 • Fix: Include target fixed effects where possible; add state-year HHI of bidders as control; re-estimate on cross-state targets only.

T3 Weak instruments or over-identification violations.  
 • Fix: Report first-stage F-statistic; run Kleibergen-Paap rk statistic; perform Hansen J over-identification test dropping each instrument in turn.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)        # fast OLS / 2SLS with FE
library(sandwich)      # VCov
library(lmtest)

# 1. Data loading
dt  <- fread("acq_master.csv")          # one row per acquisition
stat <- fread("state_AT_laws.csv")      # state-year statutes
peer <- fread("peer_Gindex.csv")        # state×year peer averages

# 2. Merge & variable construction
dt <- merge(dt, stat,  by = c("state_incorp","fyear"), all.x = TRUE)
dt <- merge(dt, peer,  by = c("state_incorp","fyear"), all.x = TRUE)

dt[, high_protect := as.integer(Gindex >= 14)]
dt[, CAR := CAR_3day]                   # –1,+1 window

# Controls
dt[, ln_assets  := log(total_assets)]
dt[, q_ratio    := TobinsQ]
dt[, cash_ratio := cash / total_assets]
dt[, year       := factor(fyear)]

# 3. 2SLS specification
iv_formula <-   
  CAR ~ Gindex + ln_assets + q_ratio + cash_ratio | 
         (SATS + peer_Gindex) + ln_assets + q_ratio + cash_ratio

est <- feols(iv_formula,
             data = dt,
             fixef = ~ gvkey + year,          # firm and calendar-year FE
             cluster = ~ gvkey + year)        # 2-way clustering

summary(est, stage = 2)                       # second-stage output
kpr <- kpr_iv(est)                            # Kleibergen-Paap F

# 4. Robustness: OLS vs IV & alternative outcome (BHAR 1-yr)
ols <- feols(CAR ~ Gindex + ln_assets + q_ratio + cash_ratio | gvkey + year,
             data = dt, cluster = ~ gvkey + year)

bhar1 <- feols(BHAR_1yr ~ Gindex | (SATS + peer_Gindex),
               data = dt, fixef = ~ gvkey + year,
               cluster = ~ gvkey + year)

etable(ols, est, bhar1, se = "cluster")
```
The code assumes `acq_master.csv` already contains CAR, BHAR, G-index, and firm-year identifiers.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory (free-cash-flow hypothesis) predicts that greater insulation weakens managerial discipline, so acquisitions by highly protected bidders should create less value (lower CAR).  Prior studies show average bidder CAR ≈ 0% to –1%.  I expect a 1-SD (≈ 4-point) increase in G reduces CAR by roughly 0.5 ppt; moving from bottom to top tercile (~9-pt swing) would lower CAR by 1–1.5 ppt.  For a $10 bn acquirer this equals ≈ $100–150 m in shareholder wealth.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV design)  
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)

C1 Strong first stage (F > 10) …………………… 1  
C2 Exclusion restriction believable ……………… 0.5  
C3 No correlated omitted shocks (FE, controls) … 0.5  
C4 No interference / SUTVA………………………… 1  
C5 Proper standard-error clustering ……………… 1  

Total = 4/5.  Primary concern is the exclusion restriction; addressed via over-ID tests and multiple robustness checks.
